description: Somos estudiantes de Ingeniería Mecatrónica y desarrolladores de Parral creando un navegador 3D para el reto Lunar Landing Site Navigator. Usamos datos reales de la NASA (topografía LOLA y efemérides SPICE) para evaluar zonas seguras de alunizaje en el Polo Sur lunar, analizando relieve, iluminación solar y enlace directo con la Tierra. Buscamos sumar compañeros con interés en UI/frontend, análisis de datos o preparación del pitch final.
summary:
LUNARIS is an interactive, science driven desktop application developed by JEBS-Systems to make lunar south pole exploration and preliminary landing-site assessment more accessible to students, enthusiasts, educators, and researchers.

Our platform combines NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data with NAIF SPICE astronomical calculations to explore lunar terrain, assess surface slope and roughness, and examine solar illumination and Earth visibility across different observation periods.

Unlike static lunar maps, LUNARIS introduces a temporal dimension to exploration. Users can select a location, configure mission parameters, and compare environmental conditions across multiple future dates. During testing, we identified a candidate location with favorable model based assessments across a 28 day comparison window, demonstrating the value of time-dependent analysis.

LUNARIS addresses the challenge by transforming complex scientific datasets into an intuitive 3D environment that supports education, exploration, and preliminary site investigation.

By making lunar data easier to understand and interact with, LUNARIS encourages scientific curiosity, promotes data-driven thinking, and helps users explore not only where lunar exploration could take place, but also when conditions may be favorable.
details:
LUNARIS: Making Lunar Exploration Accessible Through Science and Technology

1. Project Overview

LUNARIS is a functional desktop application developed by JEBS-Systems to make lunar south pole exploration more accessible, interactive, and scientifically meaningful.

Our project addresses the challenge of understanding the complex environmental conditions of potential lunar exploration sites by bringing real lunar topography, astronomical geometry, and temporal analysis into a unified three dimensional environment.

Rather than simply displaying the Moon as a static map, LUNARIS allows users to investigate how the conditions of a particular location change over time.

The platform is primarily designed for education, scientific outreach, space enthusiasts, and exploratory research, while also offering useful capabilities for preliminary lunar site assessment.

2. How LUNARIS Works

Users explore an interactive 3D representation of the Moon, navigate the south polar region, and select locations either directly on the map or by entering geographic coordinates.

They can then configure an observation date and evaluation duration to investigate three main factors:

  • Terrain characteristics: local elevation, slope, and surface roughness.
  • Solar illumination: estimated sunlight conditions over the selected observation period.
  • Earth visibility: geometric conditions relevant to potential direct Earth communication.

Our scientific engine processes lunar elevation data derived from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), including digital elevation models with nominal spatial resolutions of 10 and 60 meters per pixel.

For astronomical calculations, we integrate NAIF SPICE, which provides the geometry needed to evaluate the relative positions and directions of the Sun and Earth at different times.

LUNARIS combines these datasets to produce site assessments that users can explore through the interface.

The application also incorporates historical Artemis III candidate-region information as geographic context, allowing users to explore areas associated with lunar south pole mission planning.

3. Our Key Innovation: Exploring Time, Not Just Location

One of LUNARIS's most distinctive capabilities is its multi date comparison system.

Traditional terrain exploration focuses primarily on geographic location. However, the Moon's south polar environment introduces an important temporal dimension, particularly because of its low-angle solar illumination and changing observation geometry.

LUNARIS allows users to evaluate the same selected site across multiple future dates and compare the resulting conditions.

During our testing, we identified a candidate location that received favorable model-based assessments across the sampled dates of a 28 day forward comparison window.

This demonstrates the importance of studying temporal opportunities alongside geographic characteristics.

Our central idea is simple:

Exploring the Moon is not only about understanding where a location is, but also how its conditions evolve over time.

4. Technology and Software Architecture

LUNARIS was developed using a modular architecture that separates the user interface, application services, and scientific computations.

Desktop application and visualization

  • React 19 and TypeScript for the interactive interface.
  • CesiumJS and WebGL for three-dimensional lunar visualization.
  • Tauri v2 and Rust for native desktop integration.
  • Vite for frontend development and bundling.

Application backend

  • C# and ASP.NET Core on .NET 10.
  • HTTP APIs for communication between the application and scientific services.

Scientific computation

  • Python and FastAPI.
  • SpiceyPy and NAIF SPICE for astronomical geometry.
  • Rasterio for processing lunar elevation rasters.
  • PyProj for geospatial coordinate transformations.
  • NumPy for numerical analysis.

Deployment and infrastructure

  • Containerized backend services using Docker.
  • Docker Swarm for service orchestration.
  • Traefik and HTTPS for secure service access.
  • Linux-based server infrastructure.

The software follows modular design principles, including separation of responsibilities and maintainable interfaces, allowing scientific components to evolve independently of the visual application.

5. Creativity and Design Considerations

Our creative approach combines scientific computation with an intuitive, visually engaging exploration experience.

We focused on making technical information understandable without requiring users to operate specialized scientific software directly.

Several considerations shaped the project:

  • Scientific traceability: using established lunar datasets and astronomical computation tools.
  • Geospatial consistency: accounting for lunar coordinate reference systems when combining different datasets.
  • Temporal exploration: enabling comparisons across dates rather than limiting users to isolated evaluations.
  • Accessibility: presenting complex information through an interactive visual environment.
  • Modularity: separating visualization, application logic, and scientific processing.
  • Transparency: distinguishing preliminary analytical results from independently validated mission assessments.

LUNARIS evaluates selected environmental and geometric factors; it does not attempt to replace the comprehensive engineering verification required for an actual lunar landing.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

LUNARIS aims to bridge the gap between publicly available space science data and the people who want to understand and explore it.

For education, the platform offers an interactive way to introduce students to planetary geography, astronomical geometry, remote sensing, and scientific computing.

For space enthusiasts, it makes lunar exploration more engaging by allowing users to investigate real geographic locations and compare different observation periods.

For technical and scientific exploration, it provides a foundation for examining candidate locations and identifying periods worth investigating through more detailed analysis.

The platform also demonstrates how modern software engineering can transform complex scientific datasets into accessible educational tools.

7. Our Vision

We envision LUNARIS as an extensible platform for lunar science education, interactive exploration, and preliminary spatial-temporal analysis.

Future development could incorporate additional environmental variables, more detailed terrain-dependent visibility analysis, uncertainty quantification, and independent validation against scientific reference products.

Our goal is to encourage scientific curiosity and provide an accessible starting point for understanding the challenges of lunar exploration.
